data.title: Say vs Tell
data.description: Learn when to use 'say' and 'tell' so you can report speech naturally and accurately.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: SAY focuses on the words spoken. TELL usually needs a person (tell someone).
sections.explain: Use SAY to report what was spoken. Use TELL when you include the listener (tell someone something).

words.word: He said he would call me back later.
He told he would call me back later.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: TELL + person is common: tell me, tell her, tell them.
sections.explain: TELL normally takes an object (a person). Without a person, SAY is usually the natural choice.

words.word: She told me the meeting was cancelled.
She said me the meeting was cancelled.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: SAY something; TELL someone something.
sections.explain: SAY does not take a direct person object (not 'say me/him/her').

words.word: What did you say to your manager?
What did you say your manager about the problem?

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: If you name the listener, TELL is often best.
sections.explain: With a named listener, use TELL + person. SAY needs 'to' before the person.

words.word: I told Sarah I was running late.
I said Sarah I was running late.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: SAY can introduce a quote; TELL generally does not.
sections.explain: For direct quotes, SAY is the natural reporting verb. TELL is usually followed by information, not a quoted sentence.

words.word: He said, "I’m not ready yet."
He told, "I’m not ready yet."

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: TELL is common for giving advice/instructions to a person.
sections.explain: Use TELL when the focus is giving information to someone. If you use SAY, you normally need 'to' before the person.

words.word: They told us to take a different route.
They said us to take a different route.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: Future reporting: said/told work like other tenses.
sections.explain: SAY reports the content; TELL needs a person. Both can be used in future forms if structured correctly.

words.word: I’ll tell you the results as soon as I know.
I’ll say you the results as soon as I know.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: SAY something to someone.
sections.explain: If you want to include the listener with SAY, use 'to': say something to someone.

words.word: Please say it again more slowly.
Please tell it again more slowly.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: TELL is used for secrets/true information to a person.
sections.explain: TELL is natural with 'the truth', 'a secret', 'the story' when there is a listener (me/him/us).

words.word: He finally told me the truth.
He finally said me the truth.

sections.title: Say vs Tell
sections.summary: SAY can be used without a listener when the content matters.
sections.explain: Use SAY when the listener is not named and you focus on the message (what was said).

words.word: She didn’t say why she was upset.
She didn’t tell why she was upset.

data.title: Good vs Well
data.description: Learn when to use 'good' (adjective) and 'well' (adverb/health) so you can sound natural and accurate.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: GOOD describes nouns. WELL describes actions (or health).
sections.explain: Use GOOD for a thing/person. Use WELL for how something is done (adverb) or to mean 'healthy'.

words.word: She speaks English very well.
She speaks English very good.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: WELL can mean 'healthy'.
sections.explain: After 'feel', WELL often means healthy; GOOD can describe mood but is less precise for health.

words.word: I don’t feel well today.
I don’t feel good today because I’m ill.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: GOOD modifies nouns.
sections.explain: Use GOOD before a noun (good idea, good plan).

words.word: That’s a good suggestion.
That’s a well suggestion.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: WELL modifies verbs.
sections.explain: Use WELL to describe performance (do well, work well, explain well).

words.word: He explained the problem well.
He explained the problem good.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: Past tense still follows the same rule.
sections.explain: Even in past forms, GOOD describes nouns; WELL describes actions/health.

words.word: The presentation was good, but the timing wasn’t perfect.
The presentation was well, but the timing wasn’t perfect.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: DO WELL is common for results.
sections.explain: Use DO WELL for performance or outcomes (exam, interview, business).

words.word: She did well in the interview yesterday.
She did good in the interview yesterday.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: Future tense: same grammar.
sections.explain: Use WELL for how something will be done; GOOD for a noun quality.

words.word: I’m sure you’ll do well on the test.
I’m sure you’ll do good on the test.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: WELL after 'work' describes function.
sections.explain: Use WELL to describe how something functions (work well).

words.word: This plan will work well if everyone cooperates.
This plan will work good if everyone cooperates.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: Adjectives vs adverbs.
sections.explain: With linking verbs like 'seem', use GOOD (adjective) to describe the subject.

words.word: The proposal sounds good to me.
The proposal sounds well to me.

sections.title: Good vs Well
sections.summary: WELL can mean 'satisfactorily'.
sections.explain: Use WELL to describe how something is done (manage well, handle well).

words.word: He handled the complaint well.
He handled the complaint good.

data.title: Speak vs Talk
data.description: Learn when to use 'speak' and 'talk' for language ability, conversations, and formal situations.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: SPEAK is often about ability or formality.
sections.explain: Use SPEAK for languages/ability and formal contexts.

words.word: She speaks three languages fluently.
She talks three languages fluently.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: TALK is common for conversations.
sections.explain: Use TALK about/with for informal conversation.

words.word: We talked about the budget for an hour.
We spoke about the budget for an hour.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: SPEAK TO is more formal than TALK TO.
sections.explain: Both can work, but SPEAK TO is often preferred in formal contexts.

words.word: Could I speak to the manager, please?
Could I talk the manager, please?

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: SPEAK in public settings.
sections.explain: Use SPEAK for giving a speech/presentation.

words.word: He spoke at the conference last year.
He talked at the conference last year.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: TALK ABOUT a topic.
sections.explain: TALK ABOUT is very common for topics; SPEAK ABOUT is possible but less everyday.

words.word: Let’s talk about your options tomorrow.
Let’s speak your options tomorrow.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: SPEAK up/down is fixed usage.
sections.explain: Use SPEAK in common phrases like 'speak up' and 'speak clearly'.

words.word: Please speak up—I can’t hear you.
Please talk up—I can’t hear you.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: TALK to someone is natural for informal chats.
sections.explain: TALK TO is the default for casual conversation.

words.word: I talked to my neighbour yesterday.
I talked my neighbour yesterday.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: SPEAK for ability in future plans.
sections.explain: For language ability, use SPEAK (present/past/future).

words.word: By next year, he will speak Spanish confidently.
By next year, he will talk Spanish confidently.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: TALK is common with 'to' and 'with'.
sections.explain: TALK WITH is common for mutual conversation.

words.word: I’ll talk with you after the meeting.
I’ll speak with you after the meeting about.

sections.title: Speak vs Talk
sections.summary: SPEAK to someone about a topic.
sections.explain: SPEAK TO (person) ABOUT (topic) is standard and slightly formal.

words.word: I spoke to HR about my contract.
I spoke about HR my contract.

data.title: Hear vs Listen
data.description: Learn the difference between 'hear' (receive sound) and 'listen' (pay attention).

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: HEAR is passive; LISTEN is active.
sections.explain: Use HEAR for noticing sounds. Use LISTEN (often with 'to') for paying attention.

words.word: I heard a strange noise outside.
I listened a strange noise outside.

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: LISTEN TO is required.
sections.explain: LISTEN normally takes 'to' before the object (listen to music).

words.word: She listens to podcasts on the train.
She listens podcasts on the train.

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: HEAR about = receive news.
sections.explain: HEAR ABOUT means you learned some information/news.

words.word: Did you hear about the new policy?
Did you listen about the new policy?

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: LISTEN carefully = attention.
sections.explain: Use LISTEN for instructions/advice, because you must pay attention.

words.word: Listen carefully—you’ll need these details later.
Hear carefully—you’ll need these details later.

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: Can you hear me? = ability to perceive sound.
sections.explain: HEAR is used for whether sound reaches you (phone calls, distance).

words.word: Can you hear me clearly on this call?
Can you listen me clearly on this call?

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: LISTEN to someone (with 'to') for attention.
sections.explain: Use LISTEN TO when you pay attention to a person’s words.

words.word: I listened to his explanation and changed my mind.
I heard to his explanation and changed my mind.

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: Future: hear vs listen depends on meaning.
sections.explain: Use HEAR for noticing sound; LISTEN TO for paying attention.

words.word: If you listen to the announcement, you’ll know which platform to use.
If you hear to the announcement, you’ll know which platform to use.

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: HEAR from = receive communication.
sections.explain: HEAR FROM means you received a message/call/email from someone.

words.word: I haven’t heard from him since Monday.
I haven’t listened from him since Monday.

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: LISTEN for = try to catch a sound.
sections.explain: LISTEN FOR means you are actively waiting/trying to detect a particular sound.

words.word: Listen for your name when they call the next patient.
Hear for your name when they call the next patient.

sections.title: Hear vs Listen
sections.summary: HEAR a sound; LISTEN to content.
sections.explain: A typical contrast: hear a noise vs listen to music.

words.word: I heard the alarm, but I didn’t react immediately.
I listened the alarm, but I didn’t react immediately.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: BORROW = take from someone; LEND = give to someone.
sections.explain: Borrow something from someone. Lend something to someone.

words.word: Could I borrow your charger for an hour?
Could I lend your charger for an hour?

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: LEND takes the giver’s perspective.
sections.explain: If you give the item temporarily, use LEND.

words.word: I lent him my notes after class.
I borrowed him my notes after class.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: BORROW FROM is standard.
sections.explain: BORROW is normally followed by FROM when you name the person.

words.word: She borrowed some money from her sister.
She borrowed some money to her sister.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: LEND TO is standard.
sections.explain: LEND is normally followed by TO when you name the person.

words.word: He lent his car to a colleague for the weekend.
He lent his car from a colleague for the weekend.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: Past tense: meaning matters.
sections.explain: BORROW means you received it; LEND means you provided it.

words.word: I borrowed a book from the library yesterday.
I lent a book from the library yesterday.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: Future: lend/borrow follow the same patterns.
sections.explain: Use BORROW when you will receive; use LEND when you will give.

words.word: I’ll lend you my umbrella if it starts raining.
I’ll borrow you my umbrella if it starts raining.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: Common error: mixing direction.
sections.explain: If you need something, you BORROW it. If someone needs it, you LEND it.

words.word: Can I borrow your pen for a moment?
Can I lend your pen for a moment?

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: LEND usually needs the receiver.
sections.explain: LEND normally includes who you lend to (lend me/him/us...).

words.word: She wouldn’t lend me her laptop.
She wouldn’t borrow me her laptop.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: Borrowed items should be returned.
sections.explain: BORROW is used when you take something temporarily and will return it.

words.word: I’ve borrowed his camera, so I need to return it tomorrow.
I’ve lent his camera, so I need to return it tomorrow.

sections.title: Borrow vs Lend
sections.summary: LEND can be used with money too.
sections.explain: LEND money to someone; BORROW money from someone.

words.word: They lent us some money to cover the deposit.
They borrowed us some money to cover the deposit.

data.title: Bring vs Take
data.description: Learn 'bring' (towards the speaker/this place) vs 'take' (away from the speaker/this place).

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: BRING = towards here; TAKE = away from here.
sections.explain: Use BRING when the destination is where the speaker is/will be. Use TAKE when moving away.

words.word: Can you bring your passport to the interview tomorrow?
Can you take your passport to the interview tomorrow?

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: TAKE something home (away from here).
sections.explain: If you move something away from the current place, TAKE is typical.

words.word: Please take these documents home and read them.
Please bring these documents home and read them.

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Bring it back = return it here.
sections.explain: BRING BACK means return something to this place/person.

words.word: He brought the book back the next day.
He took the book back the next day.

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Take someone somewhere (away from here).
sections.explain: TAKE is common for accompanying someone away from the current location.

words.word: I took my parents to the airport yesterday.
I brought my parents to the airport yesterday.

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Bring to a meeting (towards the meeting).
sections.explain: If the focus is the destination where people will gather, BRING is natural.

words.word: She brought her notes to the meeting.
She took her notes to the meeting (when the meeting is here).

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Take away = remove from here.
sections.explain: TAKE AWAY is used when removing something from the current place.

words.word: The waiter took away the empty plates.
The waiter brought away the empty plates.

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Future plans: bring vs take depends on direction.
sections.explain: If you’re coming to me/us, BRING. If you’re going elsewhere, TAKE.

words.word: I’ll bring the contract to your office on Friday.
I’ll take the contract to your office on Friday (if you’re waiting there).

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Take with you = carry away.
sections.explain: TAKE WITH YOU is common when leaving this place.

words.word: Take your ID with you in case they ask for it.
Bring your ID with you in case they ask for it (when leaving here).

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Bring someone along = to here/with us.
sections.explain: BRING is natural when the destination includes the speaker/group.

words.word: He brought a colleague along to the workshop.
He took a colleague along to the workshop (when joining us).

sections.title: Bring vs Take
sections.summary: Take it there; bring it here.
sections.explain: If the destination is 'there' (not here), TAKE is typical.

words.word: Could you take this package to reception, please?
Could you bring this package to reception, please? (if reception is not here)

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: LOOK is intentional; SEE is passive/ability.
sections.explain: Use LOOK when you direct your eyes deliberately. Use SEE for noticing or ability.

words.word: Look at this graph for a moment.
See at this graph for a moment.

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: SEE does not take 'at' in most uses.
sections.explain: Say 'I see it' not 'I see at it'.

words.word: I can see the mountains from here.
I can see at the mountains from here.

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: LOOK for = search; SEE = notice/find.
sections.explain: LOOK FOR means search actively. SEE means you notice something.

words.word: I’m looking for my keys—have you seen them?
I’m seeing for my keys—have you looked them?

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: SEE someone = meet/visit.
sections.explain: SEE can mean meet/visit (see a doctor, see a friend).

words.word: I saw the dentist last week.
I looked the dentist last week.

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: LOOK like = appearance.
sections.explain: Use LOOK like to describe appearance (look tired, look like rain).

words.word: You look tired—did you sleep enough?
You see tired—did you sleep enough?

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: SEE what you mean = understand.
sections.explain: SEE is used for understanding (I see what you mean).

words.word: I see what you mean, but I still disagree.
I look what you mean, but I still disagree.

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: Future: look at vs see depends on intention.
sections.explain: You LOOK at something deliberately; you SEE something when you notice it/it becomes visible.

words.word: I’ll look at the report tonight and give feedback tomorrow.
I’ll see at the report tonight and give feedback tomorrow.

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: LOOK after = take care of (fixed phrase).
sections.explain: LOOK AFTER is a set phrase meaning take care of.

words.word: Could you look after the kids on Saturday?
Could you see after the kids on Saturday?

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: SEE if = check/discover.
sections.explain: SEE IF means check/discover information (see if it works).

words.word: I’ll see if the shop is still open.
I’ll look if the shop is still open.

sections.title: Look vs See
sections.summary: LOOK at vs SEE the difference.
sections.explain: LOOK AT is a deliberate action; SEE is the result/ability.

words.word: Look at the two versions and see which one is clearer.
See the two versions and look which one is clearer.
